scoreNote: Strong (5): grants the real, often transformative benefits of studying abroad, then shows that the sweeping word 'all' ignores cost, circumstance, field, and the student's own engagement; balanced and well organized.

sentences.text: Study abroad is often sold as a transformative rite of passage, the one semester that changes a young life forever.
From this enthusiasm the statement draws a sweeping conclusion: that all college and university students would benefit from spending at least one semester studying in a foreign country.

Study abroad genuinely enriches most students who undertake it, but the word all overreaches, for the benefit depends on circumstance, field, and the individual, and for some the cost outweighs the gain.
There is no denying the real value of studying abroad.
Living in another country forces a student out of familiar routines and immerses her in a different language and culture, an experience no classroom at home can fully reproduce.
A semester abroad can sharpen a foreign language, build independence and confidence, and replace secondhand stereotypes with firsthand understanding of how other people actually live.
For students of language, international relations, art, or history especially, such exposure is not a luxury but an extension of their study, broadening the very perspective their field demands.
For many students, then, a semester abroad is among the most valuable parts of a degree.
However, to say that all students would benefit ignores how differently they are placed.
For many, a semester abroad is simply unaffordable, and the debt or lost earnings it brings can outweigh whatever rewards it offers.
A student working to support a family, or one already stretched by tuition, may find that months away cost more than they are worth in money, time, and opportunity missed at home.
Others carry obligations — caring for relatives, holding a job, finishing a tightly sequenced program — that a semester overseas would disrupt rather than enrich.
And for some fields a semester away from laboratories, clinical placements, or studio work can set a student back rather than move her forward.
A benefit that depends so heavily on one's circumstances cannot honestly be called universal.

sections.role: Body — The benefit is not automatic

sentences.text: Moreover, even when a student can go, the benefit is not automatic.
A semester abroad rewards the student who engages with it, but one who travels only to keep to familiar company and habits may gain little beyond a change of scenery.
The real growth comes from venturing out, struggling with a new language, and forming genuine ties to a place, none of which the mere fact of being abroad ensures.
For a reluctant or unprepared student, the same months might be spent anxious and disoriented, learning less than a focused semester at home would have taught.
The opportunity benefits the student who seizes it, not every student who is handed it.
In conclusion, the statement rightly celebrates an experience that transforms many students, but wrongly extends that promise to all of them.

Studying abroad offers real and sometimes life-changing rewards, yet those rewards depend on a student's means, situation, field, and willingness to engage, so the honest claim is that most students who can go and throw themselves into it will benefit, not that every student would.
Encourage study abroad widely, but do not pretend it is the right semester for everyone.
